note: Phase 10B Section 13: memory-capacity ladder, SmolLM2-360M, Vulkan, --gpu-layers auto. Raw per-row data in gpu_memory_pressure5_360m.jsonl.
device: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650, 4096 MiB total VRAM

max_full_offload_context_found.q5_1: between 180000 and 220000 (degrades to a much smaller partial count than q5_0 at 220000 -- 4 vs 18 layers -- consistent with q5_1 costing more bytes/layer)

findings: Ordering at every ctx matches the byte-cost ordering exactly: q4 < q5_0 < q5_1 < q8 < native in failure order (native/q8 fail first, q4 fails last).
Both Q5 variants meaningfully extend the usable-context range vs Q8: at ctx=131072-180000, Q8 either partially or completely fails while both Q5 formats keep the model fully GPU-resident.

Q5_1's partial-offload degradation at ctx=220000 (4/32 layers) is much steeper than Q5_0's (18/32) at the same context -- the two formats' failure curves are not identical even though their byte budgets are close (37.5% vs 34.375% of native).

Q4 remains the only format with any GPU residency left at ctx=260000 (23/32 layers) -- consistent with Phase 10A's finding that Q4 has the largest memory-pressure advantage, now shown to be larger than either Q5 variant's.
conclusion: Q5 (either variant) is a real, meaningful improvement over Q8 for memory-constrained/high-context GPU scenarios, but does not close the gap to Q4's memory-pressure advantage -- Q4 still wins on raw context-capacity extension. The trade-off is therefore genuinely three-way: Q4 for maximum context capacity, Q5 for a middle ground, Q8/native for best quality.
